content:
The Sequences & Series chapter is a high-yield part of the CAT Quantitative Aptitude section, and a favourite in XAT, SNAP, NMAT and CMAT too. This guide explains what CAT Sequences & Series tests, the formulas and shortcuts worth memorising, the mistakes that cost marks, and a free 10-question online test you can take right now.

Take the quiz below first, read the explanation for anything you miss, then use the chapter e-book at the end for full, exam-level practice.

What CAT asks on Sequences & Series

Arithmetic, geometric and harmonic progressions, sums of series, and the AM ≥ GM ≥ HM relation.

Key formulas & shortcuts

  • AP: aₙ = a+(n−1)d, Sₙ = n/2[2a+(n−1)d].
  • GP: aₙ = arⁿ⁻¹, Sₙ = a(rⁿ−1)/(r−1); S∞ = a/(1−r) for |r|<1.
  • Σn = n(n+1)/2, Σn² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.
  • For positive numbers, AM ≥ GM ≥ HM.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using the AP sum formula for a GP (or vice versa).
  • Applying S∞ when |r| ≥ 1.
  • Off-by-one in the number of terms.

quiz.title: CAT Sequences & Series Practice Quiz
quiz.intro: Ten CAT-pattern questions. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Positive numbers α,β,γ are in A.P. If α x²+2β x+γ=0 and x²+2px+1=0 ( p≠1 ) have a common root, then (α)/(γ), p, (γ)/(α) are in
questions.explanation: Since 2β=α+γ, the first equation factors with root x=-1 (rejected as p≠1 ) and x=-γ/α. Using the common root in the second gives 2p=(α)/(γ)+(γ)/(α), i.e. p is the mean — so (α)/(γ),p,(γ)/(α) are in A.P.

questions.q: Let α,β be the roots of x²-x+p=0 and γ,δ the roots of x²-4x+q=0. If α,β,γ,δ are in G.P., then the integral values of p and q respectively are
questions.explanation: Let the G.P. be A,AR,AR²,AR³. From A(1+R)=1 and AR²(1+R)=4, R²=4. Taking R=-2 (integral p,q ) gives A=-1, p=A²R=-2, q=A²R⁵=-32.

questions.q: The sum 1²+2·2²+3²+2·4²+5²+2·6²+·s for even n is (n(n+1)²)/(2). For odd n it is
questions.explanation: Replacing the even- n formula by the odd-count adjustment gives the standard result (n²(n+1))/(2) for odd n.

questions.q: The sum of the first 20 terms of the sequence 0.7, 0.77, 0.777,… is
The sum of the first 2n terms of an A.P. is x and the sum of the next n terms is y. Its common difference is
questions.explanation: S₂ₙ=x and S₃ₙ=x+y. Subtracting the averaged forms: 2a+(2n-1)d=x/n and 2a+(3n-1)d=2(x+y)/(3n). The difference gives nd=(2y-x)/(3n), so d=(2y-x)/(3n²).

questions.q: If consecutive numbers a,b,c,d are in A.P., then abc, abd, acd, bcd are in
questions.explanation: Dividing each by abcd gives (1)/(d),(1)/(c),(1)/(b),(1)/(a). Since a,b,c,d are in A.P., these reciprocals are in A.P. too, so the original numbers (their reciprocals scaled) are in H.P.

questions.q: If the roots of x³+bx²+cx+d=0 are in A.P., then b,c,d satisfy
questions.explanation: Let roots be p-q,p,p+q; then 3p=-b⇒ p=-b/3, and p is a root, so p³+bp²+cp+d=0. Substituting gives 2b³+27d=9bc.

questions.q: An A.P. has 2n terms. The sum of terms in even positions is P and in odd positions is Q. The n th term of the A.P. is
questions.explanation: The n odd-position terms a₁,a₃,…,a₂ₙ₋₁ have average aₙ (mean of first and last), so Q=n aₙ⇒ aₙ=Q/n.

questions.q: The numbers log_b a, 1+log_b a, 2+log_b a+log_a b are in
questions.explanation: Let t=log_b a. The terms are t, 1+t, 2+t+(1)/(t). Then (1+t)²=1+2t+t²=t(2+t+(1)/(t)), the G.P. condition, so they are in G.P.

faq.q: When does an infinite GP have a finite sum?

faq.a: For positive numbers, AM ≥ GM ≥ HM, with equality when all the numbers are equal.
